run.market_summary: Three themes matter right now. (1) The US–Iran conflict is escalating in the Gulf. Iran has struck US sites in Kuwait and Bahrain, and the US has hit an IRGC missile site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Yet crude (USO -0.9% over 5 days) and defense stocks (ITA -3.8%) have not risen, so either the market doubts the threat to supply or it is waiting for a real disruption. (2) The Fed has turned hawkish. Traders price a 95% chance of a December hike after strong retail sales, Waller has floated a 50bp 'shock', and the dollar is at a 19-month high. Interest-rate-sensitive assets are already falling (ARKK -8%, IWM -4%). (3) Chip export controls are tightening: Nvidia has halted China shipments, and controls now reach Southeast Asian data centers. Semiconductor stocks are already down 5–8% this week, so much of the obvious move has happened. Ahead of the Trump–Xi–Putin summit, trade headlines could swing either way. I'm keeping the book small and avoiding several versions of the same bet.

ideas.thesis: Iran is attacking US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain, and the US has struck Qeshm, right on the Strait of Hormuz. Crude itself is down 0.9% this week while energy stocks rose about 2%, so crude has the most room to catch up if the attacks reach shipping or Gulf infrastructure.

This is the cleanest way to trade the hawkish Fed. Strong retail sales and Waller's '50bp shock' talk have pushed the dollar to a 19-month high, and the Gulf conflict adds safe-haven demand for dollars.

New US limits on AI chip exports to Southeast Asian data centers, after controls were already widened toward China, close off a growth channel for AI accelerators. AMD is down only 2.3% versus 5–6% for chip-equipment makers, and a hawkish Fed is pressuring high-valuation stocks.

Target posted its best sales growth in five years and raised guidance, and US retail sales were strong. Yet the stock is down 1.4% over 5 days, which leaves room for the typical slow drift higher after a beat-and-raise quarter, independent of the macro themes.

The war with Iran is active, with drone and missile attacks on US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain. That uses up interceptors and missile-defense stock that will have to be replaced, and Lockheed makes the PAC-3 and THAAD interceptors. The 2.1% drop this week gives a better entry point.

analysis.headline: The indexes split. A proposed CMS anti-fraud rule ("CRUSH") sent UnitedHealth down 10% and dragged the Dow lower, while crude, gold, copper and bitcoin sold off together. Amazon (Anthropic IPO), Target (earnings) and AMD lifted consumer stocks and the Nasdaq, even though Nvidia gave back its earnings pop.
analysis.narrative:
The index numbers were small and hid the real story, which was inside sectors and commodities. SPY fell 0.3% (z -0.2) and QQQ rose 0.4%, both normal moves. The Dow fell 1.1%, mostly because of UnitedHealth. UNH dropped 10.2% (z -5.7) on 3.5x normal volume, nearly all of it during the session. This was the second day of selling after CMS proposed the CRUSH rule, which expands Medicare Advantage audits and lets CMS claw back improper payments. CMS puts the savings at about $90bn over 10 years, and the clawbacks could reach back to payment year 2018. Humana, Elevance, Cigna and Alignment fell with it. Merck also fell 3.9% after it dropped nemtabrutinib, which pushed XLV down 2.2% (z -1.7).

The second theme was a broad commodity selloff that ignored the Gulf war headlines. WTI fell 4.5%, almost all after the open, as the API's overnight build of about 5.3m barrels was followed by an EIA report showing crude, gasoline and distillate stocks all rising. WTI dropped to about $82, its lowest since late August, even as Iran hit US sites in Kuwait and Bahrain and the US struck Qeshm. That took XLE down 3.3%, with CVX -4.7%, OXY -4.9% and XOM -4.0%. Gold fell 3.5% (z -2.2) and closed below $3,800 for the first time in over a year. Copper hit a seven-month low on the LME, and FCX fell 7% after an Erste downgrade. Bitcoin lost 3.9% and MSTR 6.4%. The usual story is the hawkish Fed: odds of a December hike near 95%, Waller's "shock" 50bp comment, and the dollar at a 19-month high. That fits gold's slide before the open. It fits less well during the session, when the 10-year yield fell 5bp and the dollar was flat, which looks more like hedge-fund-style selling of crowded commodity and debasement trades.

Tech reversed. Nvidia opened 2.4% higher after beating and raising, then fell 5.2% to close down 2.9%. Overhangs: the SEC probe, the leadership vacuum after Huang's exit, the Alibaba workaround report, its halt of China shipments, and the push in Congress to add chip-export bills to the defense bill (NDAA). SMH followed: up 1.65% at the open, down 1.74% during the session. Money stayed in the chip names that had been hit harder. AMD rose 5.3% after falling 13% over the prior two sessions, with analyst upgrades, and AVGO rose 3.6%. Amazon rose 3.8% because its Anthropic stake (about 14.7%, worth roughly $150bn) gets priced when the IPO lists Thursday. Target rose 4% on 3.1x volume after its best sales growth in five years and higher guidance. Together they lifted XLY 1.8% and XRT 2.3%.

Across assets the day was mixed, not risk-off. VIX fell 3.5% and long bonds rallied, but breadth was weak (5 of 13 sectors up), and the benchmarks are still down about 4% over five days. The S&P is near a five-month low.

analysis.cross_asset_read: Not a clean risk-off day. VIX -3.5%, TLT +0.8%, the 10-year -4bp to 5.07%, and the dollar +0.27% (all of it before the open). If this were a rates shock, yields would be up and growth stocks down; instead yields fell during the session as oil collapsed. Gold, copper, bitcoin and crude all fell during the session while the dollar was flat. That is liquidation of commodity and debasement positions plus bearish oil data, not a flight to safety. The Gulf war risk premium is not being priced: crude, LMT and NOC all fell as attacks continued. Equities rotated by sector rather than moving as one: health care and energy were sold, consumer discretionary bought. That points to stock-specific news (CMS, EIA, Anthropic, TGT), not macro beta.

axis_realized.note: The CMS CRUSH proposal is a healthcare crackdown. UNH -10%, XLV -2.2%, managed care broadly lower.
API/EIA builds and the IEA surplus outlook loosened supply: WTI -4.5% to ~$82, XLE -3.3%, despite the Gulf war.
Hawkish Fed repricing pressured gold and firmed the dollar before the open, but long bonds rallied during the session, so the net effect was mixed.
Overhang helped erase Nvidia's earnings pop, but AMD and AVGO rose, so it was not a sector-wide hit.

model_grade.summary: Poor: 2 of 5 trade ideas worked (TGT clearly, UUP slightly). The model's top themes, geopolitical escalation and energy supply tightening, were contradicted: oil fell 4.5% and defense stocks fell. It missed the day's biggest move, the CMS CRUSH rule hitting managed care, even though UNH had already fallen 5.4% on Tuesday.
got_right: LONG TGT: +4.0% on the beat-and-raise follow-through
LONG UUP: +0.27%, dollar held its 19-month high on the hawkish Fed
Hawkish monetary policy view: consistent with gold falling below $3,800 and dollar strength
The call that the chip-export-control move had already largely played out was right: SMH ended flat
got_wrong: LONG USO: -2.9%. The Gulf escalation thesis lost to inventory builds and the IEA surplus view, and the 'crude catch-up' never came
SHORT AMD: AMD rose 5.3% as a bounce and on the Nvidia read-through. Shorting after a 13% two-day drop into a peer's earnings was poorly timed
LONG LMT: -2.1%. The war-replenishment thesis is not being priced
geopolitical_conflict +0.58 as the top theme: it did not move prices
Rates-sensitive assets falling: IWM rose 0.4%, TLT rose 0.8%, and yields fell despite Waller
missed: The CMS CRUSH proposed rule hitting UNH, HUM and XLV. This was the largest move in the model's universe, and the first day of selling was already visible
The Anthropic IPO rerating AMZN (and the XLY lift)
Weekly EIA data as an oil catalyst: the API build was already out overnight
A broad hard-asset liquidation: gold, copper (FCX), bitcoin and MSTR

lessons: Give scheduled weekly data (EIA Wednesday, API Tuesday night) explicit weight in energy calls. When the API shows a big build, don't go long crude on geopolitics alone.

Discount geopolitical escalation as an oil or defense driver when crude and ITA have already ignored several days of attacks. Treat that divergence as evidence that the risk premium is absent, not as 'room to catch up'.
Add a healthcare_policy scan for proposed CMS/HHS rules. A first-day drop of 5% or more in managed care with the comment period still open often continues on day two.
Avoid shorting a stock into a close peer's earnings after a sharp drawdown (AMD down 13% in two days before NVDA reported). Read-through risk is skewed to a bounce.
For large IPOs, flag the listed stakeholders (AMZN, GOOGL for Anthropic) as event-driven longs or catalysts.
A hawkish Fed does not equal higher long yields when oil is collapsing. Check the oil/breakeven channel before calling rates-sensitive shorts.
